steps.en: What you see: The aortic valve sits in the centre as three thin cusps that open to a triangle in systole and close to a Y in diastole. Around it lie the right atrium, the tricuspid valve, the right ventricular outflow tract and the pulmonary valve in front, with the interatrial septum behind.
Landmarks to confirm: Do not accept the view until each of these is on screen.
Common mistakes and how to correct them: Each mistake below comes from the view catalogue with its correction.
Normal values and stenosis thresholds: Peak aortic velocity above 4 m per s means severe stenosis.
Mean transaortic gradient above 40 mmHg means severe stenosis.
Aortic valve area below 1.0 sq cm means severe stenosis.
Keep the Doppler beam within 20 degrees of flow, since angle error understates velocity.

Pitfalls: A heavily calcified valve shadows its own cusps, so count commissures in diastole when the valve is closed and still. Never grade stenosis from the two dimensional image alone; the Doppler gradient and the valve area decide.

Common mistakes and how to correct them: Oblique cut through the valve that makes three cusps look like two. Correct it by fanning through the valve slowly and accepting only the plane where all three commissures meet in diastole.
Missing the left main origin by sitting too low. Correct it by tilting slightly toward the base and looking just above the left coronary cusp in systole.
Right ventricular outflow tract crowding the near field. Correct it by tilting a touch toward the apex so the valve centres and the outflow tract thins.

todo.en: How to get it: Place the probe at left sternal edge, third intercostal space, tilted to the base.
Point the probe marker toward the left shoulder, about two o clock.
Rotate clockwise by about ninety degrees from the long axis without sliding. If the valve looks bicuspid in systole, fan slowly through it, since an oblique cut hides the third commissure.
Freeze the image only when every listed landmark is on screen at once.

remember.en: Line up continuous wave Doppler through the aortic valve for stenosis gradients.

q.en: How do you reach the aortic short axis from the long axis?

o.en: Rotate clockwise by about ninety degrees in the same space
Tilt the probe tail toward the left shoulder

why.en: Rotation by about ninety degrees from the long axis opens the short axis at valve level.

q.en: A patient has a mean transaortic gradient of 46 mmHg with a valve area of 0.8 sq cm. What grade is this?

why.en: Both the gradient above 40 and the area below 1.0 meet severe thresholds.

q.en: The Doppler beam sits 40 degrees off the jet. What happens?

why.en: Angle error always understates velocity, so realign within 20 degrees.

q.en: When is the best moment to count aortic cusps?

o.en: Diastole when the valve is closed

why.en: Closed cusps in diastole show all three commissures meeting at the centre.
